people.name: Kelly Chavez
people.title: Managing Director
people.persona: Kelly Chavez holds the firm's word to a client. She signs the retained agreements, decides what Northgate will and will not promise on a search, and is the last read on anything that describes the practice to an outsider. Her writing is warm at the open and short-winded after that, numbered wherever there is more than one thing to say, and it ends by naming the next step rather than trailing off. She talks about candidates by their current role and never by name, and she expects the same from everyone.

people.name: Sandra Fuentes
people.title: Principal
people.persona: Sandra Fuentes runs searches end to end and is the one both sides call when a process wobbles, the client who wants a slate sooner and the candidate wondering whether to keep taking the calls. She sets the context in a sentence and then says the thing, in plain long sentences with no ornament on them, and her status notes lead with where the search actually stands rather than with how much activity there has been. She is warm with people and blunt about a specification that will not attract the person the client says they want.

people.name: James Grant
people.title: Principal
people.persona: James Grant writes his client work under his full name and answers to Jim everywhere inside the firm, which is where most of his writing lives: the running notes, the session minutes, the quick line to a colleague about how a finalist is leaning. He orders things before he says them, so his minutes move through attendees, decisions, and owners in the same sequence every time, and they catch the reservation somebody voiced in passing as faithfully as the decision the room reached. With clients he has known for years he is on first names quickly; about candidates he stays formal, on the theory that discretion is a habit and not a policy.

people.name: Jeffrey Patterson
people.title: Senior Consultant
people.persona: Jeffrey Patterson carries the searches for clients who want a consultant in the room rather than a process. He gives a line of context and then leads with the answer, in short paragraphs a busy reader can take in on a phone, and he would rather send a second note than pad the first. He came up through the research side and it still shows: he will not put a name in front of a client until he can say precisely why it belongs there.

people.name: John Chang
people.title: Research Associate
people.persona: John Chang is the associate who takes the minutes, and he takes them literally: who attended, what was settled, who owns the next step. He writes formally and in short sentences, without decoration, which makes his record the one people go back to when two recollections disagree. In a session he asks more than he answers, and most of what he asks is about scope.

people.name: James Weiss
people.title: Office Manager
people.persona: James Weiss keeps the back office running and owns the firm's quarterly numbers, which he assembles the same way each time so that a comparison across a year means something. He writes in a correct, faintly formal register with the qualifications left in, and his notes end by naming what he needs and when he needs it, which is why they get answered. He is the one who notices that a search has been open longer than the plan said it would be, and he says so mildly, in writing, to everyone concerned.

people.name: David Weiss
people.title: Research Associate
people.persona: David Weiss maps the market for a search: who holds the job now, where they sit, and which of them would actually take the call. He works through a list in order and writes the same way, leading with the conclusion and then laying the supporting detail underneath it in the sequence he gathered it. He describes a prospect by role and sector rather than by name in anything that will circulate, and, sharing a surname with a colleague elsewhere in the firm, he has learned to sign his own work in full.

people.name: Jason Bell
people.title: Research Associate
people.persona: Jason Bell does the first pass on a new search: reading the specification, building the long list, turning up the people who are not obvious. He writes fast and short in internal threads and tidies it considerably before anything reaches a client. He is good on the phone with a prospect who is not looking, and his notes from those calls are the part of the file the consultants actually read.

people.name: Nicole Donovan
people.title: Research Associate
people.persona: Nicole Donovan is the associate the consultants route work through, and the file shows it: the kickoff memo, the session minutes, the note confirming a slate review. She writes quickly and without waste, in sentences that run on a little because she is thinking as she goes, and she is meticulous about who was copied on what. When a finalist withdraws, she usually drafts the careful version of that news before a principal puts a name to it.

people.name: Larry Russell
people.title: Research Associate
people.persona: Larry Russell works the hard end of a search list, the roles where the obvious people have already said no. He is patient with a slow process and comfortable going back to somebody who declined once, which is temperament more than technique. His written record is thin by choice: he would rather make the call and then summarize what he learned in a handful of lines, warmly and without overselling it.

people.name: Mary Parker
people.title: Research Associate
people.persona: Mary Parker does the verification that keeps a slate defensible: what a prospect actually owns today, and where the story a resume tells goes thin. She writes in short flat statements, often numbered, and she keeps what she confirmed strictly apart from what she was told. The consultants have learned that when her note hedges, the hedge is the finding.

people.name: Heather Meyer
people.title: Research Associate
people.persona: Heather Meyer is the newest of the research associates and still asks the question the rest of the room has stopped asking, which has already caught a bad assumption in a search specification. She writes with more energy than economy, in plain concrete language, and she is getting better at cutting it back before she sends it. She is quick at desk research and genuinely curious about the industries the firm searches in, which makes her useful early in an engagement.

timeline.summary: Firm moved into its current office.
